title: Gut comfort and mood in a longitudinal cohort
text: We followed a cohort of adults reporting digestive symptoms over twelve weeks. Higher self-reported gut comfort was associated with better mood on validated scales. The association held after adjusting for sleep and physical activity. Mood improved on days when gut comfort was higher, though the design cannot establish that comfort causes the mood change.

title: IBS comorbid with anxiety and depression: a cross-sectional study
text: Among patients with irritable bowel syndrome, comorbid anxiety and depression were common. Greater gut discomfort correlated with lower mood scores in this population. The authors caution that the cross-sectional design precludes any causal or directional claim between gut comfort and mood.

title: The gut-brain axis: a narrative review
text: This review summarises proposed mechanisms linking the gut microbiome to mood and affect via the vagus nerve, immune signalling, and microbial metabolites. Evidence in humans remains largely correlational, and the review notes that intervention studies are sparse and heterogeneous.

title: Daily step count and sleep duration in office workers
text: We examined whether daily step count predicts sleep duration in a sample of office workers. Higher step counts were weakly associated with longer sleep. The study did not measure gut comfort, mood, or any digestive outcome.

title: A randomised controlled trial of a probiotic on mood and gut comfort
text: In this randomised controlled trial, a multi-strain probiotic improved self-reported gut comfort relative to placebo over eight weeks. Mood scores also improved in the treatment arm, and the improvement in mood tracked the improvement in gut comfort, supporting a directional gut-to-mood pathway in healthy adults.
